content:
Although Apple has long positioned privacy as a selling point for its hardware and services, I sometimes wonder whether Apple now regrets introducing one privacy measure in particular: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

The scope of the measure is actually quite limited, yet it feels as though almost every month or two there's a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge against it. The UK is now seeing its third lawsuit over ATT — and there's something special about this one.

This article has been updated, with Apple's response appended at the end…

The personalised advertising controversy

Personalised advertising has long been one of the most contentious topics in tech. Rather than the ads we see being random products we may or may not be interested in, they are served based on our interests — using data collected from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win-win situation for everyone. Consumers see ads they might actually be interested in; advertisers get better results from more targeted campaigns; and free apps and websites that rely on advertising for revenue earn more for the same reason.

Even though the data used to serve personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice is still widely seen by many as an invasion of privacy. Even though Apple specifically developed a technology to ensure such data remains anonymous, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency was designed to address this by letting consumers choose for themselves whether to allow their data to be used to serve personalised ads. Any developer wishing to collect such data must first ask for the consumer's consent.

However, for the iPhone maker, the move has instead prompted a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, most of which focus on the allegation that Apple's own apps are not required to seek such consent. Apple has repeatedly stressed that its rules are actually consistent: the reason its own apps don't display the ATT prompt is because they don't collect the data covered by the prompt. Likewise, third-party apps that don't collect such data are also exempt from having to display the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has now faced three claims filed with the UK's relevant antitrust regulator — the Competition Appeal Tribunal. It lost the first (and is currently appealing) and the second is ongoing.

Reuters reported on the latest lawsuit filed today.

A distinctive twist

There's an interesting twist to the latest lawsuit: it has been brought by Ann Pope, a former senior official at the regulator handling the case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, is leading the lawsuit. She says Apple's policies "are causing very significant damage to businesses that rely on Apple as a gatekeeper." In a statement, Pope said: "This action is vital to safeguard the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules Apple sets are fair and even-handed, and to compensate UK businesses for the losses they have suffered."

Apple previously agreed to make eight modifications to its ATT rules across the EU following an investigation by the German antitrust regulator. In response to the latest lawsuit, Apple gave us the following response:

Over the years, many privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
